subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Paper 2: Poetry and Prose Texts and Imaginative Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How long is the Edexcel International GCSE English Language (Spec A) Paper 2 examination?
questions.explain: Paper 2: Poetry and Prose Texts and Imaginative Writing is a written examination lasting 1 hour 30 minutes.

questions.q: What percentage of the overall qualification is Paper 2 worth?
questions.explain: Paper 2 carries 40% of the total International GCSE English Language (Spec A) qualification.

questions.q: How many marks is Paper 2 worth in total?
questions.explain: Paper 2 totals 60 marks, split evenly between Section A (reading) and Section B (writing).

questions.q: Section A of Paper 2 requires students to respond to which material?
options: Poetry and prose texts from the Pearson Edexcel Anthology
questions.explain: Section A assesses reading of the anthology poetry and prose texts studied in advance.

questions.q: What type of writing is assessed in Section B of Paper 2?
questions.explain: Section B of Paper 2 requires one piece of imaginative (creative) writing.

questions.q: Which assessment objective covers understanding and analysing how writers use linguistic and structural devices to achieve their effects?
questions.explain: AO2 focuses on analysing writers' language and structural choices and their effects on the reader.

questions.q: Which assessment objective covers writing clearly with accurate spelling, grammar, punctuation and appropriate paragraphing?
questions.explain: AO4 rewards technical accuracy, sentence variety, vocabulary range and paragraphing.

questions.q: AO1 requires students to do which of the following?
options: Adapt form, tone and register for an audience
Read and understand texts, selecting and interpreting information and ideas
Use a range of sentence structures accurately
questions.explain: AO1 concerns reading comprehension: selecting and interpreting information, ideas and perspectives.

questions.q: How are the 60 marks in Paper 2 distributed between its two sections?
questions.explain: Section A (anthology reading) and Section B (imaginative writing) are each worth 30 marks.

questions.q: AO3 asks students to communicate effectively and imaginatively by adapting form, tone and register for what?
questions.explain: AO3 rewards purposeful, audience-aware and imaginative communication.

questions.q: Which best describes what 'imaginative writing' means in Section B?
options: Creative, descriptive or narrative writing that engages a reader
A comparison of two anthology poems
questions.explain: Imaginative writing is creative narrative or descriptive writing rather than transactional or analytical work.

questions.q: In poetry analysis, the term 'enjambment' refers to what?
options: A pause created by punctuation at the end of a line
A line of verse running over into the next without a pause
A regular rhythmic pattern of stresses
questions.explain: Enjambment is when sense and syntax continue past the line break without end-stopping.

questions.q: A student notes that a poet compares an idea to something else using the words 'like' or 'as'. Which device is this?
questions.explain: A simile makes an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as', unlike a metaphor which states one thing is another.

questions.q: Why does studying the anthology before the exam support success in Section A?
options: The exam supplies extra unseen extracts to replace it
Students can analyse the poetry and prose in detail through prior study
It removes the need to write about writers' techniques
It guarantees the same question every year
questions.explain: Prior study lets candidates develop detailed, evidenced analysis of the set anthology texts.

questions.q: What is the key difference between AO1 and AO2 in Section A?
options: AO1 rewards spelling; AO2 rewards handwriting
AO1 is about understanding and interpreting content; AO2 is about analysing language and structure
AO1 is only for prose; AO2 is only for poetry
AO1 concerns writing; AO2 concerns planning
questions.explain: AO1 assesses comprehension and interpretation, while AO2 assesses analysis of writers' techniques.

questions.q: When examiners refer to 'structure' in an anthology text, they mean which of the following?
options: Only the accuracy of the writer's spelling
How the text is organised, ordered and shaped, e.g. stanzas, shifts or endings
questions.explain: Structure covers organisational choices such as stanza form, ordering of events, shifts in focus and endings.

questions.q: Why is planning valuable before attempting the Section B imaginative writing task?
options: It replaces the need for accurate punctuation
It helps produce a coherent, well-shaped piece with a clear structure
It is marked separately for extra credit
It guarantees full AO4 marks automatically
questions.explain: A brief plan supports coherence and deliberate structural shaping, which strengthens AO3.

questions.q: For a Section B task 'Write about a moment of fear', which technique would most effectively build tension?
options: A long list of unrelated facts
Short, punchy sentences combined with vivid sensory detail
Repeated use of the passive voice throughout
questions.explain: Varied, short sentences and precise sensory imagery heighten pace and tension, rewarding AO3.

questions.q: A student wants to show how a poet creates a menacing mood. Which approach best meets AO2?
options: Simply retelling what happens in the poem
Quoting a specific word or image and explaining its effect on the reader
Describing the poet's life in detail
Counting the number of lines in the poem
questions.explain: AO2 rewards close analysis: selecting precise evidence and explaining its intended effect.

questions.q: To gain strong AO3 marks in Section B, a student should above all do what?
options: Write as many words as possible regardless of relevance
Craft engaging content and structure, matching form, tone and register to the task
Focus only on avoiding spelling errors
Include several quotations from the anthology
questions.explain: AO3 rewards imaginative, purposeful writing shaped in form, tone and register for the intended audience.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language (Spec A) (4EA1) specification; Paper 2: Poetry and Prose Texts and Imaginative Writing
